items.item: Q1 - fill in the average-speed column for each of the four heights
items.elicits: computing an arithmetic mean of three trial speed values for each height

items.item: Q2 - sketch a graph of average speed vs release height with labeled axes
items.elicits: plotting four computed data points and labeling both axes with the correct variable and unit

claims.supports: A teacher may conclude the student can compute an average from repeated trial measurements and construct a correctly labeled graph of the resulting values, produced individually in the room with AI blocked.
does_not_support: Does not support that the student understands why averaging repeated trials is done (reducing the effect of measurement variation) - that is a separate conceptual point this item does not ask about.

Does not support that the student can choose an appropriate, independent graph scale for a genuinely unfamiliar dataset, since the values were generated by the whole class together rather than by this student alone.
Does not support any ability to interpret or describe the trend the graph shows - that inference is what Q3/Q4 (S2c) separately test.
A visually correct graph does not by itself confirm the arithmetic in the table is correct, or vice versa, unless the two are checked against each other at scoring time.

delegation.reason: Computing the averages and hand-drawing the labeled graph must happen at the desk under supervision with AI blocked, so the visible work is the student's own.

claims.why_no_intervention: The claim is a direct compute-and-graph task and Q1-Q2 elicit exactly those two moves under supervised individual conditions; nothing further is needed.

items.item: Q3 - write a one-sentence claim about how speed relates to release height
items.elicits: stating a relational claim between two variables in one sentence

items.item: Q4 - cite at least two specific numbers from the table, including both the 10-20cm and 20-40cm doublings
items.elicits: selecting and quoting specific numeric comparisons from the table as evidence for the stated claim

claims.supports: A teacher may conclude the student can state a relational claim and back it with specific quoted values from the table, including both doubling comparisons the claim requires.
does_not_support: Does not support that the student can generate this claim from data seen for the first time, since the table values came from data the whole class collected together rather than from an unfamiliar dataset.
Does not support understanding of why the relationship looks the way it does - that is S3c, tested separately in Q5.

Does not support that the student recognizes the relationship is non-proportional rather than a simple direct increase - a claim like 'speed increases with height' passes here without signaling whether the student notices the pattern is not a clean doubling; that recognition is S4c, tested separately in Q6.
Two correctly quoted numbers do not by themselves confirm the student reasoned about what the numbers mean, only that they can locate and transcribe them accurately.

delegation.reason: The claim sentence and the two quoted comparisons must be composed by hand in the room with AI blocked, so producing them requires the student's own synthesis of the table at the point of writing.

claims.why_no_intervention: Q4 already requires exactly the two doubling comparisons the claim names, so the assessment already produces direct evidence for the full claim; nothing further is needed.

items.item: Q5 - explain why the pattern looks the way it does, using gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy
items.elicits: producing a free-form written explanation that invokes PE and KE vocabulary in connection with the height-speed pattern

claims.narrower_inference: The evidence supports that the student can produce a grade-appropriate written explanation that correctly invokes gravitational potential energy converting to kinetic energy in connection with this specific ramp pattern. It does not support that the reasoning is genuinely causal rather than a memorized template, because an open 'explain why' item cannot distinguish the two.
claims.supports: A teacher may conclude the student can write a grade-appropriate explanation that names gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy in connection with the ramp-height pattern.
does_not_support: Does not distinguish a genuinely causal explanation from a memorized, templated PE/KE sentence recited without engaging the specific data pattern, since the item is unconstrained prose rather than a check built around one controlling feature.
Does not support that the student can apply the PE-to-KE idea to an unfamiliar scenario outside this specific ramp dataset.
Does not support equal demonstration of conceptual understanding for multilingual learners, who may understand the physics but score lower for prose fluency in English.
Does not support precision beyond surface vocabulary use - e.g., whether the student could say why the speed increase is not proportional to height, which is a separate diagnostic judgment (S4c).

delegation.reason: Supervision and the AI block prevent outside help, but an open 'explain why' item can be satisfied with memorized PE/KE phrasing recited without engaging the specific pattern, so correct-sounding prose does not guarantee the causal reasoning was actually done.

claims.gap_statement: We cannot tell from Q5 alone whether the student's PE-to-KE explanation reflects genuine causal reasoning about this pattern or a memorized template produced without engaging the data.

minimum_additional_observation.item_text: Another student wrote this explanation: 'The cart goes faster from higher releases because it has more speed stored up at the top before it starts moving.' This sentence has one physics error. Identify the error in one sentence, and rewrite the explanation correctly using the terms gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy.
minimum_additional_observation.variant_rule: Swap the flawed phrase each form (e.g., 'more speed stored up,' 'more force pushing it,' 'more gravity at the top') while keeping the required correct terms - gravitational potential energy converting to kinetic energy - fixed, so every version needs the same repair.
minimum_additional_observation.conditions: proctored_in_class, individual, no resources beyond pen and paper, collected before students leave the room
minimum_additional_observation.sufficiency_line: A response counts as evidence if it names the specific error in the given sentence and rewrites it naming both gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy and the transfer between them.

items.item: Q6 - evaluate the claim that releasing from 80cm gives twice the speed of 40cm, using the pattern in the data
items.elicits: judging a proportional-reasoning claim against the observed pattern and citing specific numeric evidence to justify disagreement

claims.supports: A teacher may conclude the student can recognize that the height-speed relationship is not directly proportional and can cite the numeric pattern already established to refute an incorrect doubling claim.
does_not_support: Does not support that the student can quantify how much less than double the true value would be - only that it disagrees with exact doubling; the numeric estimate itself is what S5c tests separately.
Does not support understanding of the physical mechanism behind why the relationship is sub-proportional - that is S3c's job, not this item's.
Does not support recognition of non-proportionality in a different physical relationship, since this item is specific to this height-speed dataset.
A disagree judgment credited without the rubric actually checking the cited numbers for accuracy risks passing a correct hunch that is not grounded in the real pattern.

delegation.reason: Producing a numerically grounded disagreement in the room without AI requires reading and citing the actual table values at the point of writing.

claims.why_no_intervention: Q6 already presents the exact proportional-reasoning claim S4c names and requires the student to use the numeric pattern to disagree with it; nothing further is needed.

items.item: Q7 - predict the average speed at 50cm and explain the method used
items.elicits: producing a numeric extrapolation just beyond the measured range and stating the procedure used to arrive at it

claims.supports: A teacher may conclude the student can extrapolate a numeric prediction just past the measured range and state the method used to produce it.
does_not_support: Does not support extrapolation judgment far beyond the measured range, since 50cm is only 10cm past the last measured point (40cm) - a much larger extrapolation is untested.

Does not support recognition that predictions beyond the measured range carry more uncertainty than interpolated ones, since the item only asks for the prediction and method, not a statement of confidence.

Does not fully distinguish a numerically grounded method (e.g., extending the pattern of successive differences) from a plausible-sounding method description attached after the fact to a guessed number, unless the stated method is checked against the actual numeric answer at scoring time.
Does not confirm the student connects this prediction to the non-proportional pattern identified in Q6, since the two items are answered and can be scored independently.

delegation.reason: The numeric extrapolation and its stated method must be produced at the desk with only a calculator and paper, under supervision with AI blocked.

claims.why_no_intervention: Q7 already asks for a numeric prediction just past the measured range together with the method used to reach it, which is exactly what S5c requires; nothing further is needed.

conditions_echo: Grade 8 Physical Science, end-of-energy-unit summative, 30 minutes, individual work proctored in class with AI prohibited and enforced, calculator/paper/ruler permitted; the class collected the data table together in advance, but the analysis questions (Q1-Q7) are new to students.
reviewer_notes: Four of the five claims (S1c, S2c, S4c, S5c) are carried directly and fully by a single well-matched item or item pair under the declared supervised conditions, and nothing further is proposed for them. S3c is the exception: its evidence comes from an unconstrained 'explain why' paragraph, which can be satisfied by a memorized PE-to-KE template without confirming causal reasoning about this specific pattern; one short Diagnose item, run under the same supervised conditions, would close that gap without changing anything else about the assessment.
